notes: Pensions Ombudsman appeal on teachers' pension maladministration; legal errors in compensation and causation are clear.

key_facts: Miss Dann retired as a headmistress in 1978 but never claimed Teachers Pension Scheme benefits until after her death in 1997.
Her executors claimed arrears and complained to the Pensions Ombudsman that East Sussex and Teachers Pensions had maladministered her case.
The Ombudsman found maladministration and ordered the Department and East Sussex to pay retrospective interest on gross arrears.
The Secretary of State and East Sussex appealed on points of law only, bound by the Ombudsman's factual finding that no retirement form was sent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law under section 151(4) of the Pensions Schemes Act 1993 against a Pensions Ombudsman determination.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals allowed; the Ombudsman's determination set aside and the executors ordered to pay the appellants' costs.
enrichment.ratio: Trustees and pension administrators owe no general duty to advise members or proactively trace unclaimed benefits; maladministration findings must be causally linked to loss, and compensation must not overcompensate by awarding interest on sums the member would never have received net of tax.
legal_issues: Whether failure to trace unclaimed teachers amounted to maladministration
Whether regulation E34 permitted retrospective interest before October 1996
Whether East Sussex's alleged failure to send a retirement form caused Miss Dann not to claim
Whether the Ombudsman erred in extending time for the complaint

Hamar v Pensions Ombudsman [1996] OPLR 55
Outram v Academy Plastics [2000] IRLR 449
NHS Pension Agency v Beechinor [1997] PLR 99
In Re Barretto [1994] QB 392

notes: Long VAT best-judgment appeal; Rahman (No 2) test and tribunal procedure guidance are central and well reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: VAT best-judgment assessment appeal after Rahman
key_facts: Pegasus Birds' director pleaded guilty to VAT evasion linked to undeclared cash sales of imported birds.
Customs raised section 73 assessments totalling about £658,000 after a 42-day tribunal hearing found them not made to best judgment.
Patten J held the tribunal misapplied the best-judgment test and remitted quantum; Pegasus appealed on law and costs.
The dispute concerned whether wholly unreasonable assessments must be set aside or corrected to the fair tax due.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the High Court on the correct test for challenging VAT assessments made to the best of the Commissioners' judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed save on tribunal costs, which were remitted; assessments held properly made and quantum remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 73(1) VATA 1994, an assessment fails the best-judgment requirement only if there was no honest and genuine attempt to make a reasoned assessment; objective unreasonableness alone does not invalidate the assessment, and tribunals should focus primarily on determining the correct tax due.
legal_issues: Whether best judgment is a wholly subjective or combined objective-subjective test
Consequences when part of an assessment is vitiated
Whether European administrative-law cases alter the domestic VAT review standard
Appropriate costs order where a two-stage tribunal hearing misfired

notes: Construction adjudication enforcement refused for apparent bias; paragraph 1.11 reasoning is decisive.

enrichment.short_title: Adjudication enforcement refused for apparent bias

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: A&S Enterprises sought to enforce an adjudicator's decision ordering Kema Holdings to pay about £89,475 on a JCT design-and-build contract.
Payment turned on whether an application for payment had been made to the employer and whether architect Ernest Austin could certify.
The adjudicator convened a short-notice meeting to hear Mr Austin; the employer's key witness Mr Overend did not join the telephone link.
The adjudicator criticised Mr Overend's non-participation and said he viewed the responding party's submissions in that light.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 24 application to enforce a construction adjudicator's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment application dismissed and the action dismissed; enforcement refused for apparent bias and breach of natural justice.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator who criticises a party's submissions because a witness chose not to participate by telephone, without having clearly required that witness's oral evidence beforehand, creates a real possibility of bias and denies natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 1.11 of the decision showed apparent bias
Whether the defendant had fair notice that Mr Overend's oral evidence was required
Whether the adjudicator properly considered the defendant's quantum submissions
Validity of payment application under the Scheme where certification was disputed

notes: Consultancy commission trial; oral agreement and collateral contract issues are comprehensively resolved.

key_facts: Richard Grosvenor claimed commission from High-Point Rendel for business introductions made between 1999 and 2001.
A written agreement from 1 August 2000 provided a retainer and tiered commission for one year only.
The claimant never invoiced for commission before 2003 and disputed whether any oral commission deal existed before or after the written term.
Only introductions to Burges Salmon and SJ Berwin during the written agreement period yielded admitted commission of £1,251.58.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for commission on consultancy introductions after re-amended particulars.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant for £1,251.58 plus VAT and interest; all other commission claims and declaration application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: No oral commission agreement existed before the August 2000 written contract, no binding collateral agreement backdated commission to February 1999, and an oral agreement in August 2001 ended further commission while the retainer continued; post-termination commission was not implied.
legal_issues: Whether oral commission was agreed in 1998 or 1999
Whether a collateral agreement backdated commission to February 1999
Terms applying after expiry of the one-year written agreement
Whether introductions to Pfizer, BTP and NAO triggered commission

notes: Lease indemnity strike-out application dismissed; disclosure compliance and CPR abuse analysis are thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Strike-out refused in lease indemnity claim
key_facts: Scottish & Newcastle assigned hotel underleases to Raguz in 1982; the ultimate tenant later defaulted after a 1995 rent review.
The landlord demanded over £461,000 and Scottish & Newcastle paid about £346,000, then sought indemnity from Raguz.
Partial summary judgment had already been entered for pre-August 2000 rent; the balance turned on a support agreement with receivers.
Raguz applied to strike out the claim for persistent disclosure failures and defective formal pleadings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out the claim or make unless orders relating to disclosure and pleading.
enrichment.outcome: Strike-out application dismissed; unless orders refused; defendant directed to re-amend defence.
enrichment.ratio: Disclosure ordered by Gaunt J was given in good faith and was not illusory; earlier disclosure defects had been cured, and tactical summary judgment conduct did not justify striking out a triable indemnity claim.
legal_issues: Whether disclosure complied with the October 2003 order
Whether witness statement inaccuracies warranted strike-out
Whether the claimant concealed material from the court
Appropriateness of unless orders before pleadings were closed

notes: Article 8 judicial review dismissed; Robinson/Shen rule 18(6) and Shala delay argument clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Kosovo asylum Article 8 judicial review dismissed
key_facts: An ethnic Albanian from Kosovo claimed asylum in July 1998 but was not interviewed until March 2002 and refused asylum.
An adjudicator dismissed asylum and Article 8 appeals; the IAT refused leave to appeal.
On judicial review the claimant relied on new delay grounds not raised before the IAT, arguing he would have obtained status but for Home Office delay.
Fresh evidence suggested he would at most have received 12 months exceptional leave, not indefinite leave to remain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal against an adjudicator's Article 8 dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: New grounds in judicial review must satisfy both limbs of Robinson: strong prospect of success and readily discernible on the material before the tribunal; the Shala delay principle is fact-specific and did not apply where prompt processing would not clearly have yielded refugee status or ILR.
legal_issues: Effect of rule 18(6) on new grounds raised in judicial review
Whether Home Office delay made Article 8 removal disproportionate
Whether Shala applied to a July 1998 arrival
Whether the adjudicator failed to take a holistic family view

confidence.notes: Sullivan J's reasoning on Robinson, Shala and Razgar is detailed. Outcome and permission refusal are clear.

notes: Part 36 interest comparison on PI claim; Brooke LJ's like-with-like analysis is authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 beaten only if damages plus interest to last acceptance date exceed payment
key_facts: The claimant injured his dominant thumb at work in May 1998 and rejected a Part 36 payment of £40,000 gross in November 2001.
The county court judgment was £40,854.03 inclusive of interest accruing after the last date for acceptance.
Compared at the acceptance date, damages plus interest totalled £39,644.71, below the £40,000 payment.
The judge had awarded the claimant 70% of costs; the defendants appealed on CPR 36.20 interpretation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from county court orders on Part 36 costs consequences after personal injury trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; claimant ordered to pay defendants' costs from 3 December 2001.
enrichment.ratio: For CPR 36.20, a claimant beats a Part 36 payment only if judgment for damages plus interest up to the last date for acceptance exceeds the gross sum paid in; post-acceptance interest cannot be counted.
legal_issues: Whether post-acceptance interest counts when deciding if a Part 36 payment was beaten
Whether defendants may top up interest payments into court
Whether it would be unjust to order claimant costs under CPR 36.20(2)
Effect of CPR 36.23(4) on gross sum comparison

confidence.notes: Focused procedural point with clear arithmetic comparison and unanimous Court of Appeal reasoning.

notes: Trade mark bad faith appeal dismissed; combined Twinsectra/Gromax test applied to CHINA WHITE facts.

enrichment.short_title: CHINA WHITE trade mark refused for bad faith
key_facts: Mr Harrison applied to register CHINA WHITE for Class 32 and 33 drinks after bar manager Matt Rymer approached him.
Opponents ran the successful CHINAWHITE nightclub and had developed a house cocktail of the same name from late 1998.
Rymer had been employed to create the cocktail for the club but told Harrison he owned the name and recipe.
The hearing officer and Pumfrey J found the applications made in bad faith; Harrison appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of trade mark applications on bad faith under section 3(6).
enrichment.ratio: Bad faith under section 3(6) uses a combined test: conduct must fall short of acceptable commercial standards judged by reasonable and experienced persons in the field, and the applicant must realise honest people would regard the application as bad faith; believing Rymer did not excuse applying to monopolise a mark already used by the nightclub.
legal_issues: Whether bad faith requires dishonesty or includes sub-standard commercial behaviour
Whether the test is subjective or objective
Whether the applicant's belief in Rymer's ownership defeated bad faith
Relationship between nightclub reputation and drinks mark monopoly

notes: ASBO against child in care; conflict-of-interest guidance is the principal lasting contribution.

enrichment.short_title: ASBO against child in care: conflict guidance
key_facts: M, born 1989, was in Sheffield City Council care from 1995 and shared parental responsibility with his mother.
Serious youth offending led the housing ASBO panel to seek an order; social services reports were sceptical but the panel proceeded.
Council housing led the application while social workers were conflicted and unavailable as defence witnesses.
An interim ASBO was granted without adequate notice or social services attendance; Moses J later stayed it pending review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of ASBO proceedings against a looked-after child and an interim ASBO made in the magistrates' court.
enrichment.outcome: Substantive relief declined because the interim order had expired; judgment gave guidance on managing conflicts when a local authority applies for an ASBO against a child in its care.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority with parental responsibility for a child may apply for an ASBO but a conflict arises between public protection duties and welfare duties; the child's interests must be protected by independent social services reporting under section 22(4)-(5), separate decision-making, and court attendance without the ASBO solicitor controlling social work evidence.
legal_issues: Whether a local authority may ever apply for an ASBO against a child in care
How section 22(4) consultation applies to ASBO decisions
Procedures to avoid prejudice in court preparation
Whether an interim ASBO should have been made without notice

notes: Permission to appeal refused in estate litigation professional negligence claim; abuse of process finding upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Perotti professional negligence appeal permission refused
key_facts: Mr Perotti sued two solicitor firms and a barrister for advice given in 1993 during administration proceedings over his uncle's estate.
Retainers with each defendant ended quickly in acrimony after Perotti rejected settlement advice and accused advisers of dishonesty.
The writ was issued in April 1999; Peter Smith J entered summary judgment and struck the claim out as an abuse of process.
Perotti sought permission to appeal, seeking to re-litigate issues already decided against him in other proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against summary judgment and strike-out for abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant has no real prospect of success where competent 1993 advice against pursuing hopeless estate claims was rejected, and re-litigating issues already determined against him in other actions is an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether summary judgment was correctly entered on negligence claims
Whether the action was an abuse of process
Whether new allegations against former solicitors revived merit
Reliability of contemporaneous conference notes
